recTjh2r9ceNB4puf.Bio: Tamara Sheville is the author of the Level Plane Poem series, six volumes of illustrated verse arguing that Earth is flat, level and motionless, covering curvature, surveying, navigation and celestial observation. fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Joining InnerVerse for their first time, Tamara Sheville and Brandon Thomas are here to explore one of the most absurd deceptions in the history of psyops.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: Drawing from Tamara's background in hazardous materials, DoJ training programs and real-world chemical, biological and radiation hazard response team work, Tamara is primed to deliver a powerful truth bomb about the science of nuclear fission, why it works for power plants but will never go boom, and how the evidence from Japan's supposedly nuked cities tells a different story to the trained eye. As the co-host of the new Mysterious Universe podcast, Brandon Thomas is no stranger to fringe ideas, bringing his jovial yet razor sharp spiritual discernment to bear on the devilish details of this conspiracy. For the members we answer all the questions left on the table: the mechanics of nuclear fission and why it can't produce an explosion, the "nuclear shadows" phenomenon and why it raises serious questions, underwater tests, mushroom clouds and what actually creates those visuals, and the additional historical inconsistencies that don't line up with the official story.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Fission Explained Without the Priesthood", "body": "The whole reason for the extension is to slow down and say plainly what nuclear fission is. A neutron is fired at a uranium-235 nucleus, billiard ball style, and if it lands just right the nucleus splits and throws off two or three more neutrons that have to go hunting for nuclei of their own. Tamara adds the conditions a power plant supplies and a weapon cannot, meaning shielding, moderation, cooling and time, with water used to slow fast neutrons enough to be absorbed. The verdict they keep returning to is that heat is not detonation."}, {"title": "The Odds Get Worse With Every Generation", "body": "Tamara stacks the improbabilities using the analogies from her book. A fast neutron moving at twenty thousand kilometers per second is a putt struck far too hard to drop, the nucleus is a marble somewhere inside a stadium, and even a direct hit may scatter or simply be absorbed without splitting anything. When a split does happen it produces krypton, barium, strontium and xenon, new objects cluttering the space. Chance restates the point back to her, that each generation adds blockers rather than shots, while roughly eighty generations are needed for an exponential chain reaction."}, {"title": "Two Rocks Banged Together Over Hiroshima", "body": "Once the mechanics are on the table the official Hiroshima story gets retold in its own terms. A gun type device slammed two pieces of uranium together, it had never been tested, and it allegedly flattened a city on the first attempt after the Manhattan Project burned millions of dollars a day. Brandon points to the side by side in Tamara's book comparing the two bombs, one implosion type and one explosion type, one tested and one not, and the declassified admission that there was nowhere near enough uranium to go around."}, {"title": "Where the Photographic Evidence Falls Apart", "body": "The screen share turns to the pictures. Seversky spent days walking Hiroshima looking for a hypocenter, a bald spot, anything different, and found unsinged telephone poles and wooden buildings still standing. The famous shadows are cast by ladders, pails and a metal truck as readily as by people, and one wheel throws a shadow while the wheel beside it does not. Black smoke requires carbon to burn and fission has none, a cloud sits motionless through supposed hurricane force winds, and the mushroom cloud grandeur quietly shrinks between 1946 and 1962."}, {"title": "Carrying This Without Becoming Insufferable", "body": "The last stretch is about what to do with the conclusion. Brandon frames it as offering a butterfly idea to caterpillar minds, invoking Da Vinci's three classes of people and Churchill's definition of tact, which is telling someone to go to hell in a way that makes them look forward to the journey. Chance plays a time lapse of every alleged detonation and argues that either the world already ended or this was never a problem. Both land on the same test, that sudden imported fear is the tell that something is untrue."}]
